analysis.one_liner: Permanently bans offshore oil and gas drilling in Atlantic waters off the East Coast.
analysis.headline: The bill was never considered by the Senate committee it was sent to and died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act to bar the Interior Secretary from ever leasing areas of the Atlantic outer continental shelf — the Mid-Atlantic and North Atlantic planning areas — for oil, gas, or mineral exploration, development, or production. It would write a permanent legal prohibition into statute, taking the decision away from future administrations. The bill was introduced by two New Jersey Democrats and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal communities, beachgoers, and the tourism and fishing economies of Atlantic coast states, who would be protected from the risk of offshore oil spills and the industrial activity that accompanies drilling platforms. The bill's sponsors argued the Atlantic coast's ocean economy depends on clean water and beaches.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Atlantic coastal towns, beaches, tourism, and fishing

how_it_helps.text: Permanently prohibits the Interior Secretary from issuing any lease for exploration, development, or production of oil, gas, or other minerals in the Mid-Atlantic and North Atlantic planning areas, no matter which party controls the White House.

Writing the ban into the statute itself ('notwithstanding any other provision of this section or any other law') would override contrary instructions elsewhere in law, making the protection harder to reverse than a policy that depends on annual appropriations or presidential withdrawal.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies would be permanently shut out of drilling in those two Atlantic planning areas. To the extent those waters hold recoverable oil and gas, the nation forgoes that domestic supply, and the industry loses potential future acreage.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas companies seeking Atlantic leases

drawbacks.text: The bill forecloses domestic energy production in the Atlantic planning areas permanently, which oil and gas producers and some policymakers argue reduces future domestic supply and leaves energy resources off the table regardless of future need or improved drilling safety technology.

A statutory ban is rigid: unlike annual moratorium riders, it could not be adjusted by a future Congress weighing new drilling technology, energy price conditions, or revised spill-risk assessments without passing new legislation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is permanent protection of Atlantic coastlines and the tourism and fishing economies that depend on them, at the cost of excluding drilling from those specific federal waters. The tradeoff is real but regional: the ban covers two planning areas, not all offshore drilling, and the strongest objection is that it removes flexibility to revisit the decision if energy conditions or drilling safety change.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Sen. Jon Corzine introduced the COAST Anti-Drilling Act on May 7, 2003, joined by Sen. Frank Lautenberg as cosponsor.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources, where no further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — was ever recorded.
The 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005, and the bill died in committee without ever receiving a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies kept the Atlantic planning areas formally available for future leasing, and no protections were added. Coastal communities got nothing, though Atlantic drilling did not move forward in this period either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas producers; Atlantic coast left unshielded

for.name: Sen. Jon Corzine
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Jersey; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to permanently ban Atlantic offshore drilling and delivered introductory remarks.

for.name: Sen. Frank Lautenberg
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Jersey; cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, named on the introduction as a co-introducer.

against.name: Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on May 7, 2003 and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Only two Democrats sponsored the bill and no Republican cosponsor ever joined; the record shows no votes, so no party split can be measured.

industries.note: The bill permanently bars leasing for exploration, development, and production of oil and gas in the Mid-Atlantic and North Atlantic planning areas, removing those federal waters from the industry's future acreage. Its interest in blocking the ban ran against coastal communities' interest in spill-free beaches and fisheries.

A permanent drilling ban protects the beaches, water quality, and fisheries these industries depend on; the bill's title itself ties the ban to tourism. Their gain is the drilling industry's loss in these waters.
